etymology: Hebrew Chatsar Gaddah, “the village of Gad” or “court of fortune” — a settlement in the far south (the Negeb) of Judah, near the coast of Edom.
biblical_def: Hazar-gaddah was one of the uttermost cities of the tribe of Judah toward the coast of Edom southward, named in the great catalogue of the inheritance: “And Hazargaddah, and Heshmon, and Bethpalet” (Josh 15:27). It is a name that appears once and then falls silent, a mere dot in the dry country of the south. Yet its silence preaches. When Joshua divided the land by lot, the LORD did not overlook the least and dustiest hamlet on the edge of the wilderness; every village was numbered, allotted, and recorded, for “the land shall be divided by lot: according to the names of the tribes of their fathers they shall inherit” (Num 26:55). The very meaning of the name, a “court of fortune,” is redeemed in Israel’s theology: what the heathen ascribe to blind fortune, the covenant people ascribe to the sovereign hand that setteth the bounds of the peoples. Hazar-gaddah stands as a small witness that not one good thing the LORD promised failed; the whole land, to its farthest village, came into the hand of His people, that they might dwell in it and serve Him.
webster_summary: An obscure village in the far south of Judah toward Edom (Josh 15:27); a witness that God allotted every least town of the inheritance and forgot none.

corruption_summary: An obscure town of the south; it recovers the doctrine that God’s providence, not fortune, allots every bound of habitation, down to the least village.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The name “court of fortune” might tempt the reader to think Israel shared the pagan worship of luck and chance. She did not. The lot was cast into the lap, but the whole disposing thereof was of the LORD. What the nations round about called Gad, fortune, and set a table for, Israel confessed to be the appointed portion of a faithful God.

The principle to recover is that God determines the bounds of every people’s habitation. He “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation” (Act 17:26). There is no fortune, no blind chance, no roll of the dice outside His decree; the smallest village in the driest corner of the south was given by the same hand that upholds the stars.
roots_summary: An obscure village in the far south of Judah toward Edom; a witness that God allotted every least town and forgot none.

etymology: Hebrew Cheshmon, of uncertain meaning, perhaps “fatness” or “fruitfulness” — a town in the far south of Judah, listed once in the tribal survey.
biblical_def: Heshmon is named a single time in Scripture, set between Hazar-gaddah and Beth-palet in the roll of Judah’s southernmost cities: “And Hazargaddah, and Heshmon, and Bethpalet” (Josh 15:27). It lay in the parched Negeb, toward the border of Edom, where water was scarce and the tokens of fruitfulness few. Yet if its name indeed means fatness or fruitfulness, it stands as a quiet promise that the LORD can make even the dry south to be fat with His blessing; for it was written of the whole land that it was a good land which He had given, and the tribes were to dwell and prosper in it. The town preaches the completeness of God’s gift. When the surveyor walked the border and set down Heshmon among the rest, he testified that “there failed not ought of any good thing which the LORD had spoken unto the house of Israel; all came to pass” (Josh 21:45). The obscure town, whose story we do not know, is folded into the one great story of a faithful God who keeps covenant to a thousand generations and leaves no promise void.
webster_summary: A town in the far south of Judah, named once (Josh 15:27); its name (perhaps “fruitfulness”) preaches that God can make even the dry south fruitful and keeps every promise.

The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage.
corruption_summary: An obscure southern town; it recovers the faithfulness of God, who leaves no promise void and gives His people a goodly heritage.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. There is no modern controversy attached to a village named once in the wilderness of the south. The temptation, if any, is simply to pass it by as too small to matter — the very error the Spirit rebukes by writing its name in the everlasting record.

The principle to recover is the faithfulness of God, who forgets nothing He has promised. Joshua at the end of his life could say, “not one thing hath failed of all the good things which the LORD your God spake concerning you” (Josh 23:14). If He kept faith to give an obscure town to an obscure family, He will keep faith with every soul that trusts Him; the believer may say with David, “The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage” (Psa 16:6).
roots_summary: A town in the far south of Judah, named once; a witness to the faithfulness of God who leaves no promise void.

etymology: Hebrew Beth Pelet, “house of escape” or “house of deliverance” — a town in the south of Judah; reinhabited after the Babylonian exile (Neh 11:26).
biblical_def: Beth-palet, the “house of escape,” was a town in the southern reaches of Judah, listed among the uttermost cities toward Edom: “And Hazargaddah, and Heshmon, and Bethpalet” (Josh 15:27). It was not forgotten in the return from captivity, for the men of Judah dwelt there again after the exile, at Beth-phelet with its villages (Neh 11:26). The name itself is a little sermon. In a land where every family was appointed a refuge and the manslayer could flee to a city of refuge, and where the LORD Himself is named the refuge of His people, a “house of escape” on the frontier speaks of the God who is a hiding place from the storm. He that made this town also made a way of escape for His people out of Egypt, out of Babylon, and out of the bondage of sin; “God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble” is the confession of all who know Him. Beth-palet, small and southern, carries in its name the gospel truth that there is a house of deliverance for every soul that flees to the Lord, and none that trust in Him shall be desolate.
webster_summary: A town in the south of Judah, “house of escape” (Josh 15:27; Neh 11:26); its name preaches the God who is the refuge and deliverance of His people.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. No progressive redefinition threatens so obscure a place. Its whole message is in its name: a house of escape, a place of deliverance, standing on the dangerous southern frontier as a token of safety in the LORD.

The principle to recover is that God is the refuge of His people. He appointed cities of refuge for the manslayer, and He is Himself the true and greater refuge for the sinner fleeing the avenger of blood. The believer confesses, “The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage” (Psa 16:6), and rests in the God who kept every good promise (Josh 21:45), making a house of escape for all who come to Him.

etymology: Hebrew Bizyoth-yah, of uncertain meaning, containing the divine name Yah; a place in the south of Judah near Beer-sheba, named once.
biblical_def: Bizjothjah is one of the most obscure names in the whole survey of Judah, listed once among the towns of the south near Beer-sheba: “And Hazarshual, and Beersheba, and Bizjothjah” (Josh 15:28). Its meaning is uncertain, but the divine name Yah lies buried in it, as it lies buried in Hallelu-jah and in a hundred Hebrew names, a reminder that the covenant people carried the name of their God into the very soil of their villages. Set beside Beer-sheba, the well of the oath where Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob all called on the name of the LORD, Bizjothjah shares in that region’s memory of patriarchal worship at the southern edge of the promise. The town preaches that no place is too small, and no name too strange, to bear witness to God. When Joshua parcelled out the land, this dot on the border was written into the everlasting inheritance, and its unfamiliar name still whispers Yah, the LORD, who fixed the bounds of His people’s dwelling and left no corner of the promised land unclaimed.
webster_summary: An obscure town in the south of Judah near Beer-sheba (Josh 15:28); its name carries the divine name Yah, a witness that God’s name marks even the least village.

corruption_summary: An obscure southern town carrying the divine name; it recovers the truth that the LORD claims and marks even the least village of His inheritance.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. A name spoken once and never again invites no modern quarrel. What it invites is wonder that the covenant name of God was woven into the ordinary places where His people lived, ate, and slept, so that even a border hamlet bore the syllable Yah.

The principle to recover is that God lays claim to His whole inheritance, down to its obscurest bounds. “He cast out the heathen also before them, and divided them an inheritance by line, and made the tribes of Israel to dwell in their tents” (Psa 78:55). The Most High “set the bounds of the people according to the number of the children of Israel” (Deu 32:8); no village of the promise lay outside His care or His name.

etymology: Hebrew Iyyim, “heaps” or “ruins” — a town in the far south of Judah toward Edom, named once; possibly the same as Ije-abarim on the wilderness march.
biblical_def: Iim, whose name means “heaps” or “ruins,” was a town in the southernmost part of Judah, listed with Baalah and Azem: “Baalah, and Iim, and Azem” (Josh 15:29). It stood in the dry country toward Edom, a place of stone-heaps and rough ground. The very name is sobering, for it speaks of ruins — and the history of Israel would in time turn many a proud city into heaps because of sin. Yet at the giving of the land, Iim was no ruin but a possession, a token of the goodness of God who gave His people cities they builded not. The town preaches the two ends that Scripture sets before every people: to dwell securely in the LORD’s inheritance, or, by rebellion, to be made a heap and a hissing. Israel was warned that the same land which flowed with milk and honey would spue out its inhabitants if they defiled it as the nations had. Iim, a heap of stones on the frontier, is a standing parable that what God gives in mercy He may take in judgment, and that the only sure dwelling is with the God who keeps His covenant and His people who keep His way.
webster_summary: A town in the far south of Judah, “heaps” or “ruins” (Josh 15:29); a parable of the two ends before every people — to dwell securely, or by sin to be made a heap.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. A single-verse town raises no modern dispute. Its name, “ruins,” carries its own quiet warning, needing no controversy to sharpen it: cities become heaps, and only the LORD abides.

The principle to recover is the seriousness of dwelling in God’s land on God’s terms. He divided the inheritance by line and made the tribes to dwell in their tents (Psa 78:55), but He warned that the land would spue out a defiling people as it spued out the heathen. What was given in faithfulness (Josh 21:45) could be lost in unbelief. The believer learns to hold every earthly gift with a loose hand and to seek the city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God.

etymology: Hebrew Amam, perhaps “gathering place” or “mother-city” — a town in the south of Judah, named once in the tribal survey.
biblical_def: Amam is named a single time, first in a little cluster of southern towns: “Amam, and Shema, and Moladah” (Josh 15:26). It lay in the Negeb, the dry south country of Judah, and nothing of its story survives beyond its name in the roll of the inheritance. If the name means “gathering place,” it fits the pattern of the south, where scattered families gathered around the few wells and the walled towns for safety in a hard land. The town preaches the mercy of God in gathering a people to Himself. Israel was a scattered company of slaves whom the LORD gathered out of Egypt, planted in the land, and set in cities; and the prophets looked beyond every earthly gathering to the day when the Lord would gather His elect from the four winds. Amam, a gathering place on the southern border, is a faint early type of the great assembly of the redeemed, gathered not by their own strength but by the God who “gathereth together the outcasts of Israel” and will lose none that the Father hath given Him.
webster_summary: A town in the south of Judah, perhaps “gathering place” (Josh 15:26); a faint type of the God who gathers a scattered people to Himself.

The principle to recover is the gathering mercy of God. He cast out the heathen and made the tribes of Israel to dwell in their tents (Psa 78:55), gathering a nation out of bondage. Beyond the earthly gathering, the Lord Jesus came to gather into one the children of God that were scattered abroad, and He will send His angels to gather His elect from the four winds. Every earthly gathering-place is a shadow of that great and final assembly of the redeemed.

etymology: Hebrew Bealoth, “mistresses” or “citizens,” a plural form related to Baal (lord, owner); a town in the south of Judah, named once.
biblical_def: Bealoth is listed once among the southern cities of Judah: “Ziph, and Telem, and Bealoth” (Josh 15:24). Its name is a plural form akin to Baal, “lord” or “owner,” a word that in the Canaanite tongue named the false gods of the land. That such a word should survive in the place-names of Israel is a reminder of the world into which the LORD planted His people, a land thick with the shrines and names of Baal. Israel was commanded to drive out that worship, to break down the altars, and to teach her children that the LORD alone is God. The town preaches the sharp antithesis at the heart of the covenant: the people bore names and dwelt in places still echoing with the old idolatry, yet they were called to be wholly the LORD’s. Where Israel forgot this, she went a-whoring after Baalim and was chastened; where she remembered, she prospered. Bealoth in the south stands as a quiet caution: it is not enough to possess the land; the heart must be purged of every rival lord, for “thou shalt have no other gods before me” is the first and abiding word of the covenant.
webster_summary: A town in the south of Judah whose name echoes Baal (Josh 15:24); a caution that the land, and the heart, must be purged of every rival lord.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The town raises no dispute of its own, but its name opens onto the oldest of Israel’s dangers: the worship of Baal. That idolatry is no relic; it survives wherever men crown some created thing lord of the heart in the place of God.

The principle to recover is the exclusive lordship of the LORD. Israel dwelt in a land whose very stones bore the names of Baal, yet she was commanded to cleave to God alone. The modern heart, no less than the ancient, is a factory of idols — wealth, appetite, self, the approval of men — each a little baal demanding to be lord. The gospel calls the sinner from every such lord to the one Lord Jesus Christ, that God may be all in all.

etymology: Hebrew Naamah, “pleasantness” or “sweetness” — a town of Judah in the low country (the Shephelah); distinct from the women of the same name.
biblical_def: Naamah, “pleasantness,” was a town of Judah in the Shephelah, the low rolling country between the hills and the coast, listed in a cluster of the valley cities: “And Gederoth, Bethdagon, and Naamah, and Makkedah” (Josh 15:41). It is not to be confused with Naamah the daughter of Lamech (Gen 4:22) nor with Naamah the Ammonitess, mother of Rehoboam; this is a place, not a person. The name is a sweet one, and the Shephelah was indeed a pleasant and fruitful region compared with the dry south, well-watered and set with vineyards and grain. The town preaches the pleasantness of the LORD’s portion. David, surveying his own lot, sang, “The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage” (Psa 16:6), and every faithful Israelite could say the same of the land God gave. Yet the truest pleasantness is not the fatness of the Shephelah but the favour of God Himself, in whose presence is fulness of joy. Naamah, a pleasant town among the vineyards, is a small figure of the far greater sweetness of communion with the God who giveth His people a goodly heritage and Himself for their exceeding great reward.
webster_summary: A town of Judah in the fruitful low country, “pleasantness” (Josh 15:41); a figure of the pleasant heritage God gives, and of the sweetness of communion with Him.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. A town named once raises no modern quarrel. The only confusion to guard against is mistaking this place for one of the women named Naamah; the Shephelah town is a distinct entity, a pleasant place among the valley cities of Judah.

The principle to recover is that the LORD’s portion is truly pleasant, and Himself the sweetest of all. David rejoiced, “The lines are fallen unto me in pleasant places; yea, I have a goodly heritage” (Psa 16:6). Yet the psalm rises higher, to the LORD Himself as the portion of the soul. Earthly pleasantness fades, but in God’s presence is fulness of joy and pleasures for evermore; the believer’s truest Naamah is the favour of God.

etymology: Hebrew Baalath Beer, “mistress of the well,” also called Ramath of the south (Ramath-negeb); a town in the inheritance of Simeon, within the territory of Judah.
biblical_def: Baalath-beer, the “mistress of the well,” was a town given to the tribe of Simeon, set within the larger portion of Judah, and marked as the southern limit of their villages: “And all the villages that were round about these cities to Baalathbeer, Ramath of the south. This is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Simeon according to their families” (Josh 19:8). Its second name, Ramath of the south, means “height of the Negeb,” and it was likely a place David knew, for he sent of the spoil of Ziklag to his friends in Ramoth of the south. The town teaches a lesson in the wisdom and generosity of the tribes, for “the part of the children of Judah was too much for them: therefore the children of Simeon had their inheritance within the inheritance of them” (Josh 19:9). Judah, having received more than it needed, made room for its smaller brother Simeon; the strong bore the portion of the weak. So the body of Christ is knit together, the abundance of one supplying the lack of another, that there be no schism in the body but that the members have the same care one for another. Baalath-beer, a well in the dry south, is a small monument to that brotherly sharing of the inheritance.
webster_summary: A town of Simeon within Judah’s portion, also called Ramath of the south (Josh 19:8); a monument to Judah sharing its abundance with its smaller brother Simeon.

corruption_summary: A town of Simeon within Judah; it recovers the brotherly sharing of the inheritance, the strong making room for the weak, as members of one body.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The name begins with Baalath, “mistress,” an owner-word like Baal, but here it names only a well in the wilderness. No modern controversy attaches; the lesson lies in how Judah and Simeon divided the land.

The principle to recover is the sharing of inheritance among the brethren. Judah’s portion was too much, so it made room for Simeon within its bounds (Josh 19:9). This is the pattern of the church, where he that gathered much had nothing over, and he that gathered little had no lack; where the abundance of one supplies the want of another, that there be equality and no schism in the body of Christ.

etymology: Hebrew Eshan, “support” or “leaning-place” — a town in the hill country of Judah near Hebron, named once.
biblical_def: Eshean was a town in the hill country of Judah, in the district about Hebron, listed once with Arab and Dumah: “Arab, and Dumah, and Eshean” (Josh 15:52). If its name means “support” or “leaning-place,” it preaches by its very name the deepest question of the soul: on what does a man lean? Israel dwelt among fortified towns and leaned often on the arm of flesh, on horses and chariots and the strength of walls; and the prophets rebuked her for it, crying that they which stay on the LORD and lean not on their own understanding shall be established. The town in the hills, a place of support, becomes a parable of true and false trust. He that leaneth on his own righteousness, his own wisdom, or the props of the world, leans on a broken reed that will pierce his hand; but he that leaneth on the LORD, as the bride in the Song came up from the wilderness leaning upon her beloved, shall never be moved. Eshean, an obscure support-town of Judah, points the heart to the only sure support, the everlasting arms underneath the people of God, on whom the believer may lean with all his weight and never fall.

corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. No modern quarrel touches a town named once in the Judean hills. Its name, “support,” simply presses the ancient question: on what does the soul lean? and the answer is not obscure but everywhere in Scripture.

The principle to recover is that the soul must lean on the LORD alone. Israel leaned often on horses and walls and the arm of flesh, and was rebuked; but the righteous lean on God and are established. As the bride came up from the wilderness leaning upon her beloved, so the believer leans his whole weight on Christ, resting not on his own righteousness or strength, but on the everlasting arms which are underneath, and which never fail.
